rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The three-item list when there is one finding.** Packaging a real finding with two minor ones implies a parity that does not exist and makes the reader sort them.
rules.says: Do not pad a single real finding into a three-item list with minor ones; one finding is written as a sentence, not a list.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The bolded lead-in on every paragraph.** Emphasis on everything is emphasis on nothing;
rules.says: Do not put a bolded lead-in on every paragraph of a reply, because it makes a reply look scannable while being flat.
rules.enforcer: stop-guard.mjs (refuses a bolded lead-in on four consecutive paragraphs)

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **Self-deprecation attached to a finding that stands without it.** When the misreading IS the lesson, say it.
rules.says: Do not wrap a finding that stands on its own in self-deprecation or apology; say the misreading only when it is itself the lesson, and when the number is the lesson the number is the reply.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **"Worth naming" / "worth having" / "worth recording."** A claim of importance in place of the importance. Say the thing or drop it.
rules.says: Do not write phrases like 'worth naming', 'worth having' or 'worth recording' in place of the substance; say the thing itself or drop it.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The status recap when nothing moved.** Branch, staging, production, "nothing running" — real the first time, noise every time after,
rules.says: Do not repeat a status recap (branch, staging, production, nothing running) when nothing has moved since the last one.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **A manufactured next step, so the reply has an ending.** If there is nothing to ask for, the reply ends without asking for anything.
rules.says: Do not invent a next step or request just to give a reply an ending; if there is nothing to ask for, the reply ends without asking.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **Two of these are refused mechanically now** — the bolded lead-in on four consecutive paragraphs, and a reply sectioned under three or more bold headers — by [`stop-guard.mjs`](stop-guard.mjs),
rules.says: A reply may not carry a bolded lead-in on four consecutive paragraphs or be sectioned under three or more bold headers, and the other slot habits, which no pattern can tell from honest twins, stay the session's own responsibility to avoid.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The test for all of them: would this sentence survive if the reader could only read three lines?** What survives is the finding and what it costs.
rules.says: Apply to every sentence the test of whether it would survive if the reader could read only three lines, keep the finding and what it costs, and cut the rest rather than spend the reader's attention on a shape.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: The owner is iPad-first and often driving. So
rules.says: Standing fact: the owner works iPad-first and is often driving, and sessions shape their output and steps for that.
rules.live_quote: The owner works outdoors on an iPad — avoid a full-field `#FFFFFF`: keep the page
rules.missing: The standing fact that the owner is iPad-first and often driving, and the instruction that sessions shape their output and steps for that. The live line is scoped to page colour only; 'often driving' is stated nowhere live.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - One step at a time. No desktop-required steps unless every alternative is exhausted.
rules.says: Give the owner one step at a time and never a desktop-required step unless every alternative is exhausted.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - Deliver FINISHED work — no drafts, no pseudo-code. Iterate privately, hand over the finished thing.
rules.says: Hand the owner finished work only, with no drafts and no pseudo-code, iterating privately before handover.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - The owner's time is expensive; runner time and your time are free.
rules.says: Standing fact: the owner's time is expensive while runner time and the session's own time are free, so spend the latter to save the former.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - **NEVER RENDER A TABLE OR ANY GRID LAYOUT IN ANYTHING NOAH READS.** Markdown tables do not display on an iPad
rules.says: Never render a table or any grid layout in anything the owner reads (chat replies, commit messages, PR bodies, NOTES.md, plan files, changelogs and any other artifact they open), using headed lists, short prose or one fact per line instead, because tables arrive as unreadable noise on an iPad.
rules.enforcer: docs-check.mjs over every tracked .md, run from the hub and never forked; it cannot see a chat reply, so that part is on the session
rules.live_quote: - No table or grid where the owner reads.
rules.missing: The named scope (chat replies, commit messages, PR bodies, NOTES.md, plan files, changelogs, every artifact the owner opens), the alternatives (headed lists, short prose, one fact per line) and the reason (iPad shows pipe-and-dash noise, content lost).

rules.heading: Tables: the gate
rules.quote: **Enforced by [`docs-check.mjs`](docs-check.mjs)** over every tracked `.md`,
rules.says: The no-table rule is checked by docs-check.mjs over every tracked .md file, and that check is run from the hub and never forked into another repository.

rules.heading: Tables: what the gate cannot see
rules.quote: A rule nothing enforces is a preference (§16.8). The gate cannot see a chat reply, so that part is still on the session.
rules.says: The table gate cannot see a chat reply, so keeping tables out of chat replies stays the session's own responsibility; a rule nothing enforces is only a preference, so do not treat an unenforced part as optional.
rules.live_quote: - No table or grid where the owner reads.
rules.missing: The statement that the table gate cannot see a chat reply, so that part is on the session, and that a rule nothing enforces is a preference and not optional. Only the bare prohibition is live.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: A comparison that feels tabular is written as a list per item, never as columns.
rules.says: A comparison that feels tabular is written as a list per item, never as columns (the owner's ruling, 2026-07-29, after repeated offences).
rules.live_quote: - No table or grid where the owner reads.
rules.missing: The instruction that a comparison that feels tabular is written as a list per item, never as columns. Only the bare no-grid prohibition is live.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - **ANYTHING THE OWNER IS MEANT TO PASTE, RUN OR CARRY ELSEWHERE IS ONE FENCED CODE BLOCK.** A handoff prompt, a command, a config, a message to send on
rules.says: Anything the owner is meant to paste, run or carry elsewhere (a handoff prompt, command, config, message to send on) ships as a single plain-text fenced code block, not as prose, a blockquote or formatted markdown.
rules.live_quote: - Anything meant to be pasted is one fenced block.
rules.missing: The scope 'run or carry elsewhere' (live says only pasted), the named cases (handoff prompt, command, config, message), plain-text with a copy control, and the ban on prose, blockquote or formatted markdown.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The test is not "is it readable" but "what happens to it next".** If the answer is paste, it is a block.
rules.says: Decide whether something is a fenced block by what happens to it next, not by how readable it looks: if the next action is paste, it is a block, and do not optimise for the reading over the using.
rules.live_quote: - Anything meant to be pasted is one fenced block.
rules.missing: The test that the choice is made by what happens to the thing next and not by how readable it looks, and the warning not to optimise for the reading over the using. Also the 'run or carry elsewhere' scope and the ban on prose or blockquote.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: *Enforced for host lists by:* `stop-guard.mjs` (Q-HUB-293), which refuses a reply where a line outside a fenced block holds three or more hostnames or a line inside one holds two or more,
rules.says: A host list goes one host per line in one fenced block; a reply is refused if a line outside a fenced block holds three or more hostnames or a line inside one holds two or more (hostnames ending in com, org, net, gov, edu, io, dev, uk, science or info).
rules.live_quote: (§2):** ONE fenced code block, bare hostnames, one per line, **ordered so the
rules.missing: The mechanical refusal (three or more hostnames on a line outside a fenced block, two or more inside) and its hostname endings list. Live never.md:372 says stop-guard never refuses a stop. The one-per-line fenced-block form is live only for asking for a denied host.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: - **A REPORT ENDS IN DECISIONS OR IT ENDS IN NOTHING.** A list of everything outstanding is not a handover, it is work handed back.
rules.says: A report must not close with an inventory of everything outstanding for the owner to sort; it ends in decisions or in nothing.
rules.live_quote: - Bring back to the owner only a choice that is the owner's, with the recommended option first.
rules.missing: The explicit rule that a report must not close with an inventory of everything outstanding, and that it ends in decisions or in nothing.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: So the close of any report is a SHORT numbered list of the things only the owner can settle, each written as a question with the options named and a recommendation first, answerable in one word.
rules.says: The close of any report is a short numbered list, two or three items and never more than four (rank and hold the rest), of only the things the owner alone can settle, each a question with options named, recommendation first, answerable in one word.
rules.live_quote: - Bring back to the owner only a choice that is the owner's, with the recommended option first.
rules.missing: The close as a short numbered list of two or three, never more than four (rank and hold the rest), each written as a question with options named and answerable in one word. Only 'only owner's choice, recommended first' is live.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: What does NOT go in that list: anything already settled, anything a session can do itself, anything the owner has already been told twice,
rules.says: Keep out of the closing decision list anything already settled, anything a session can do itself, anything the owner has been told twice, and the standing manual steps (metadata, the Pages project, the default branch), which are at most a status line and never a re-served to-do list.
rules.live_quote: PRACTICE IS NEVER A QUESTION.** Anything already settled in this file, in
rules.missing: The exclusions for anything the owner has already been told twice, and that the standing manual steps (metadata, the Pages project, the default branch) are at most a status line and never a re-served to-do list. 'Already settled' and 'a defect with a known fix is fixed, not asked about' are live.

rules.heading: The slots — structural habits that look like content and are not
rules.quote: **The failure it names, in the owner's terms: a long list to do with no choices to make, and nothing marking what is being answered.**
rules.says: Never close a reply with a long to-do list that has no choices to make and nothing marking what is being answered (written after three replies running closed with an inventory of outstanding work).
rules.live_quote: - Bring back to the owner only a choice that is the owner's, with the recommended option first.
rules.missing: The explicit ban on closing a reply with a long to-do list that has no choices to make, and the requirement that something marks what is being answered.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: **A PLAN THE OWNER APPROVED IS THE INSTRUCTION FOR ALL OF IT.** Not for the first phase.
rules.says: An approved plan is the instruction for all of its phases; approval is not consumed by the first deliverable and a phase boundary is a seam in the work, not a checkpoint in the permission.
rules.live_quote: 2. Put the page to the owner for approval once. After approval the work runs to its end without further asking.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: - **Never end a turn on a completed phase of a live plan.** Report what landed and start the next piece in the same turn.
rules.says: Never end a turn on a completed phase of a live plan; report what landed and start the next piece in the same turn, since the report is a side effect of working and not a stopping point.
rules.live_quote: scope. And it is not an argument for silence: report what landed and start the next item IN THE SAME TURN, which is §11c, not a new rule.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: - **"Holding for input" is a decision, and it needs a REASON that is not tidiness.** Two reasons qualify:
rules.says: Holding for input needs a reason that is not tidiness, and only two qualify: the next step is genuinely blocked on something only the owner can supply, or proceeding under either reading of an ambiguity would waste real work; wanting a nod or having just written a long report does not qualify.
rules.live_quote: - **NEVER MANUFACTURE A STOPPING POINT. THE WORK STOPS WHEN THE QUEUE IS EMPTY
rules.missing: The two qualifying reasons for holding for input (blocked on something only the owner can supply, or either reading of an ambiguity would waste real work) and the statement that wanting a nod or having just written a long report does not qualify. Live states only a general no-manufactured-stop rule, plus the need format at page.md:12.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: - **If you do stop, the FIRST line says so, in those words** — *stopping here, waiting on you for X*.
rules.says: If you do stop, the first line of the reply says so in the words 'stopping here, waiting on you for X', never buried at the end of a report.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: - **A question is not a stop.** Ask it, state the assumption you are proceeding under, and keep working on everything the answer does not block.
rules.says: A question is not a stop: ask it, state the assumption you proceed under, and keep working on everything the answer does not block, stopping with nothing delivered only where any assumption could be unsafe.

rules.heading: 11c. An approved plan is standing authority. Do not stop at its seams.
rules.quote: - **This does NOT license a new sweep.** §11b still binds: the authority is the approved plan's remaining phases, not work of your own invention.
rules.says: The standing authority of an approved plan covers only its remaining agreed phases and does not license new sweeps or work of the session's own invention: do all of what was agreed and none of what was not.
rules.live_quote: Two things this is NOT. It is not permission to start a sweep of your own —

rules.heading: 11c. Failure mode
rules.quote: **The failure mode this replaces is worse than it looks**, because it is invisible from the owner's side.
rules.says: Standing fact: a session that stops without saying so is indistinguishable from one still working, so an unannounced stop costs hours nobody was watching.

rules.heading: It has teeth now, because the paragraph did not hold
rules.quote: So the escalation is not a fifth paragraph. **[`stop-guard.mjs`](stop-guard.mjs) is a `Stop` hook**, wired in each repo's `.claude/settings.json`
rules.says: A reply that says the work is still running (for example waiting on a background poll) and does not open with the declaration 'stopping here, waiting on you for X' is refused at stop; either wait for the thing and carry on, or make that declaration the first line.
rules.enforcer: stop-guard.mjs (Stop hook, exit 2, via .claude/hooks/stop-guard.sh shim in each repo; honours stop_hook_active; fails open when the hub is not checked out beside the repo)

rules.heading: It has teeth now
rules.quote: **[`stop-guard.mjs`](stop-guard.mjs) is a `Stop` hook**, wired in each repo's `.claude/settings.json` through a `.claude/hooks/stop-guard.sh` shim.
rules.says: The stop guard is a Stop hook wired in each repository's .claude/settings.json through a .claude/hooks/stop-guard.sh shim, and it refuses the stop with exit 2, feeding its message back as the next instruction.

rules.heading: It has teeth now
rules.quote: It is narrow by design: it fires only on a reply that both admits waiting and omits the declaration,
rules.says: The stop guard fires only on a reply that both admits waiting and omits the declaration, never loops because it honours stop_hook_active, and fails open (does not protect) when the hub is not checked out beside the repository.

rules.heading: Same escalation as branch-guard
rules.quote: **This is the same escalation `branch-guard.mjs` is built on.** An instruction in a file never once refused the commit it forbade.
rules.says: Standing fact: an instruction in a file does not itself stop anything, so a rule a session must remember after hours is weaker than one the harness runs regardless (as branch-guard.mjs does for commits); do not rely on memory where a guard exists.
rules.live_quote: otherwise go stale in the tree**, which an instruction in a file never once managed.
rules.missing: The general standing fact that an instruction in a file stops nothing and a rule a session must remember is weaker than one the harness runs regardless, and the instruction not to rely on memory where a guard exists. Live states it only for generated artefacts under branch-guard.
